utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Before we begin today, Mr. Robinson, probably you remember the Chamber's oral order lifting the confidentiality of the submission from a certain country. Having heard that, that country intends to respond to your motion, and having noticed that order hasn't been implemented, I told the Registry to hold the implementation of it. Very well. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Patelski.

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you notice the presence of any military observers in Srebrenica, and if so, did you co-operate with them?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the observers various times, but I never had any contact with those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what it was that they did, what their job was?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I understood that they were present at the different meetings on behalf of the battalion staff reporting to the superior military officers, and on various occasions they negotiated with, for example, the different parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know their names? Did you know them personally?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know the observers by name, and I don't know them personally either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they help the Dutch Battalion in any way?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite honestly, I can't answer that because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your amalgamated statement, in paragraph 10, you say that you saw Serb trenches and that you saw Serb snipers operating. Where were Serbs within the range of snipers? What is the range for an ordinary sniper?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you ask me what the range is of a sniper, I can't tell you exactly because that's not my area of expertise. All I can tell you is that I saw them at that time, so before the fall of the enclave. That was quite a bit before the enclave was about to fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have your statement before you, your amalgamated statement? Well, we can call it up in e-court in order to be able to see paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it in front of me, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the Prosecution to provide a hard copy of the amalgamated statement to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's here through e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have it in front of me. I can read along.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at paragraph 10 now. Where were the Serbs in a position to use snipers against the Muslims at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was doing my work, that was at the observation post, that was generally in the north-westerly direction at the top of the hills, and from that position the snipers were able to do their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the distance involved?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the distance from where I was to the sniper?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I mean the distance, between the Serb positions and the Muslim houses. This is what I put to you, that the distance was far too great and that that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't guess about the distance, and I don't want to guess. All I can say that I saw those snipers as -- as did my colleagues several times from where I was. So the sun was regularly in that line of vision. And next shots fell from that -- when shots were fired from that location, we wound up with injured people several times at our observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, at which point during the year is the sun at south-west on the northern hemisphere? When is the sun at north-west?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Never, Mr. Patelski, never. The sun can only be on the east, south-east, south and south-east, on the northern hemisphere that is. Do you know the name of any victim?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have any names because they were all residents of the enclave, and of course I didn't know them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So they were within the agreed boundaries of the enclave, the area that you patrolled; right?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the victims?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Muslim village, yes, that Muslim village where people live and who were allegedly within the range of Serb trenches and Serb fire. They were on the separation line, and the Serbs were on the other side outside the enclave; right?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the sniper was on the outside of the enclave, but his range was sufficient to claim victims, and we wound up with those victims at the entrance to our observation post, and we treated them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Give us one such case. Tell us who was wounded, what this person's name is, when this happened.

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I can't give you a date. I don't know that. And second, I certainly can't give you a name because I don't know those people by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you report about that?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of our duties if we observed anything out of the ordinary, incidents or whatever. We would always draft a report, and we would submit that report to our commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is there such a report that civilians were hit by sniper and that you took care of them?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When something like that has happened, we report that by radio to our OPs room, and all reports arrive there, and we did so. Subsequently, it was forwarded to the commander so that he could use that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The ones that came later were reports in writing; right?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the observation post we did everything from one minute to the next. When we observed, we would make notes. We would take notes about that, and we would report very urgent matters immediately. Some reports were done every other hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we have the Serb positions there, and then we have your station, and then there are the Muslim villages. Were the Muslim villages between you and the Serbs or were you between the Serbs and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have the Serb positions on the one hand and the Muslim village on the other hand. Was this Muslim village closer to the Serbs than you were or was your observation post closer?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were reasonably close to the assorted villages. So if you ask me that question, then I think that we were close to the villages. When victims fell, they reached us fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, your observation post, was it on the periphery? Were you closer to the Serbs or were the villages closer to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well from, my observation post, of course, we were adjacent to the different houses across the street. There were some houses. The closest post to us was Yellow Bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But my question is: Were you closer to the Serbs or were Muslim villages closer to the Serbs? Who was deeper into the enclave, you or the Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How can you not know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Patelski, if you are shown a map, do you think you can mark the positions of those snipers and the victims and yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Then I propose that you show me the normal map and not the aerial photograph. I would be able to point it out better that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will leave it to the parties. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to that. I would kindly ask that we be provided with a map that the witness would understand. Actually, Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it is for you, if you're minded to put that to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll find it. I thought that the OTP had it -- well, the OTP tendered something, so I thought that perhaps we could have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 19 and otherwise you use this form, this form of syntax: [In English] "They would go near the house and throw a grenade into it. After that, they would enter the house with the dogs," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] Tell us, please, the civilian population, was it there when the Serbs advanced or had the civilian population left beforehand? Had they gone to Potocari beforehand?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When on the day concerned the Serb troops entered the enclave, of course the day before something happened from the south, so various refugees went in the direction of Potocari to our camp, and when we were confronted with the incursion from the north, various people were still present in their homes, so on the north side of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you say that in some village the Muslim civilian population was there to see the arrival of the Serb troops; right?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if about that. From our observation posts we can't see everything in the enclave, only a small portion of it. But I don't think the population sat there waiting for the arrival of the Serb militia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, look at what you say in paragraph 19: [In English] "They would go near the house," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] And then you would hear gunshots and screams or whatever it was that you said. Shooting and screams. And you say that you knew that a number of Muslim people were still living in those houses and that you had the impression that the people had been killed in those houses. Mr. Witness, you are testifying about things you had seen. Are you saying that you saw some civilians actually staying there and being killed by the Serb troops once they arrived?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the towers, from the tower of my observation post I could see very clearly that the Serb army entered and started to purge all the homes. That's what I saw. Not only I. My colleagues saw that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Purge all the homes from what?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time the Serb army entered and marched to the south or to the base, well, all houses were looked over. Not simply looked over to see whether there were still people there. There were still people there. And as I described in item 19, I stand behind that because I saw it. I not only saw it, I also heard it. And I was not the only one who saw it. My colleagues saw it too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how many such houses did they enter? They -- you say that they went to the next house and then they would repeat the same thing; right?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's entirely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then the people in the next house, they would just be sitting there waiting for the Serbs to come and kill them; right? And then the third house and then the fourth house, and then the fifth house. People would just be sitting in their homes listening to screams and moans that you allegedly heard as well, and shooting, and you say that you saw and heard that, and they did nothing. They just sat there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I object to these forms of questions. They're not questions at all. They're argument. It's the defendant's case and he goes on and on. It's argumentative. This witness should not be subjected to it, and the defendant should ask this witness a simple question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you can ask the witness what he saw, not formulating as a submission, as Ms. West indicated, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, but here it is, paragraph 19. That's what he says. They enter one house, then shooting would be heard and screams, and then they'd leave that house and then go into the next house and then another one and yet another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Patelski, you say that. You say that people were just sitting there waiting, whereas these other people were purging, as you say, the houses in that way. Just tell me, is this what you're actually saying?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's aren't my words. Those are your words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And are these your words: [In English] "They would then move to the next house. This went on for a couple of hours, and at one particular moment I remember seeing people coming out of at least one house." [Interpretation] For several hours that was going on. That is what you describe in paragraph 19, Serbs entering houses one by one, killing people, and in all these other houses people are just sitting there and waiting for their turn to come. Is that your position, sir? Is that what you saw and heard?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, once again, those are not my words. Those are your words. People don't wait to be killed. And what I saw was that the Serb army on the -- simply marched forward, including with their dogs, and they entered. It doesn't mean that they entered each house. They entered along a line. So conceivably they might take over two or three houses at a time. They would enter it. They would barge into the houses and shoot. I heard screaming. Grenades were thrown in, and at -- by the time they were done, the army set those houses on fire, and to them that was a sign that they were done once the house was ablaze, and they would continue their march. That's how you should see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that lasted for a few hours; right?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my impression, it took a few hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. How many victims were there in those civilian villages?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know, Mr. Patelski, that the Muslim authorities had sent their representatives to every village and ordered that civilians go to Potocari, whereas able bodied military-age men were told to make a break-through to Tuzla? They never met with resistance from civilians. They sometimes met with resistance from people who had hidden weapons in haystacks, and those people resisted when the weapons were to be seized from them. Do you know that the Muslims were told to leave before the Serbs came?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just have a cite for this? I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all the witnesses we've heard confirmed this, including the Dutch witnesses. And a Muslim witness also said that the authorities had ordered civilians to go to Potocari. Look at 0.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the accused can proceed with that question. The witness can answer as far as he knows.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can answer to this question is that at the moment the enclave fell I was at Observation Post Papa, and I was taken hostage there too. There were some things that I saw, and they all appear in my statement, and everything else that happened at that time, of course, I don't have any way of knowing about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Patelski, from that tower at that OP Papa, how far were the Muslim houses that were set fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be tens of metres. So between 20 and 200 metres from where I was located, what I could see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we then see 23519. That's the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And we would kindly ask you to mark the relevant points. Page 8, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just enlarge, or rather, zoom in on the area of the enclave, the border in purple.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you now please mark your position. Just wait for the usher to give you the pen.

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position at that moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's OP Papa, the north side of the enclave, i.e., the entrance to the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please mark it with number 1.

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where was the Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my position and then there are a few villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that's very close to the UN base in Potocari; right?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would be between the base and the observation post where I was at the time, OP Papa. Both to the left and to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's almost inside the base; right? Very close.

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's within 1 kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell us then, how many victims were there, and in which report can we find it, the kind of victims you described?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which victims do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Victims in houses. You described the civilian population remained in their homes, that Serbs came with dogs, troops came inside houses, threw grenades in. You heard screaming. How many victims were there, and in which report can we find it?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I don't know how many victims there were, and second, I can't tell you what the reports were. I cannot make a statement about that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you, Mr. Patelski, that there is no such thing in UN reports, although it happened, if we are to believe you, right outside the UN base, how come it's not in any report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, it's self-evident the witness can't answer a negative question like that. First of all, you're making a submission, i.e., giving evidence that there are no reports; and secondly, you're asking the witness to comment on why something hasn't happened. It's -- it's an example of how you use your time very badly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please follow up on that? Everything that we saw through all particularities, all troop displacements, everything concerning possible victims, everything that we saw, we communicated that directly via our radio connection. At the time we still had that radio connection, which was subsequently taken from us by the Serb army because of the fact that we were taken hostage at the time and couldn't do anything any more, but everything that we saw we reported over the radio, and what happened with that afterwards I have no idea, but I stand by the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In your statement, Mr. Patelski, you stated that you had the impression that people had been killed in houses. So you were not sure that people were actually killed inside the houses. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When I say my impression, what I mean is that I didn't see it, physical, visual contact with the victims and the people, but I did hear that people were screaming and yelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Patelski. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Patelski, did the Muslim side have trenches between you and the Serbs, or maybe behind your back or right in front of you? Were there any Muslim trenches facing the Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly how the trenches lay, but I know that the Serbs brought in reinforcements, that preparations had been in progress for a few days, so a few days in advance, reinforcements replaced, and at the same time, of course the Muslims weren't crazy. They started working on their own defence. So they also dug trenches and prepared for the things that lay ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, could you kindly put number 2 for those markings indicating to the Muslim villages and then ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. And could you kindly put your initials and today's date at the bottom of the map, which is 16th of January.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ordinarily my handwriting is better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That will be the next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2005, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say Muslims were not fools and of course they prepared themselves, do you know what kind of military resources Muslims had in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that because I didn't see them. I didn't see what types of resources the Muslim warriors had available to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Wasn't one of the tasks of UNPROFOR to keep the enclave demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but again, I have to base myself on my level at the time and where I was at the time. I was a soldier one, so part of implementation aspects, so all I can speak about is something that I know and that I saw, and everything else is speculation on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever been told that carrying weapons is forbidden in the enclave and there should be no military formations? Did you ever receive such an assignment, and were you ever informed that there were military units there and that people were carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that you weren't supposed to bear arms at the time. In the compound in the city of Srebrenica there was a weapon collection point where all weapons were surrendered. That's what I know about that. And once again, when I was in service during the fall of the enclave, I did not observe any troop displacements as far as the Muslims were concerned. All I can speak about is what I saw and all the troop movements were by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it then also your task to -- or mainly your task to observe the conduct of the Serbs and neglecting the DutchBat mission to preserve demilitarisation and monitor it?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had to report everything out of the ordinary. It doesn't matter which group this concerned. Everything out of the ordinary concerning displacements, incidents, whether by the Muslims or the Serbs, that didn't matter. Everything relevant, which meant everything, we had to report everything out of the ordinary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask for your understanding now, because I did not notify in advance one exhibit. It's a short video, 40582. Could we see it now, please, from 16:45.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this area, Mr. Patelski?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks familiar, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's close to your observation post. Can you see the Muslim trenches there and Muslim soldiers hiding there, finding cover from fire?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was filmed from the Serb side, and you see the Serbs standing in front of Muslim trenches taking cover, and they are pointing to the cameraman where the Muslim trenches are. So the enclave was surrounded with Muslim trenches; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. If I watched the video properly, then that recording was done near Potocari, our big base, and when the enclave was about to fall. I wasn't there because I was at OP Papa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Isn't that close?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's about a kilometre between Potocari and Observation Post Papa, and from our post you can't see all of the kilometre, of course. So everything in the vicinity of OP Papa was easily perceptible to us, and everything deeper into the enclave I can't tell you, and I'm not going to make any statement about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You saw soldiers here that you described exactly that way, long haired and bands around their heads, a mixture of military and civilian clothing. So did you see, did you notice that they had these hair bands or bandannas?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the Muslims had at least three tanks in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you knew that the Serbs were carrying anti-tank weapons, and you spoke about that in your statement, in your evidence before this Tribunal in response to a question from the Prosecution. That was your testimony. Let me see. In 2000, on 6th June, number 30099299. Did you see the Serbs carrying antitank weapons?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I saw is that Serb militias, and they were several Serb militias, were armed in various ways, including those items.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you also saw some Chetniks with Chetnik insignia and emblems, and they were long-haired young men; right?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a variety of different appearances. For example, indeed long-haired men, bandannas, those things, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, you mentioned you were hostages. How did that happen? On what day, and in what form at OP Papa?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the 12th in the morning. Anticipating this matter in February, somewhere between February and March, you'll find it in my statement, the observation commander, Mr. Jovo, had already told us, that's me and my commander, that in the summer the Serb army would carry out an offensive. We reported that immediately. On the 11th the south was attacked, and then in the north on the 12th we -- we were overrun. Before that, we were being fired at for a few days. We were in a bunker. And then the enclave was shot at from outside and the shooting was directed at the population in the enclave. And immediately from the early morning on the 12th, Mr. Jovo sent us report, because we had a line. That's also in my statement. So we had telephone contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] Wait a minute. Let's explain this. How many victims were there among the civilian population where the shells were falling? Let just be precise.

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't report anything about that because I don't know the exact figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were in the bunker at OP Papa, and you say the fire was targeting civilian population. How can you prove that?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were in the bunkers, at the time we still had access to our communication devices, and we maintained those at all time. We were in contact with our immediate commander in the OPs room when the enclave fell at the south, and the days before concerning all the particularities concerning the shooting and the shelling, they reached us by radio communication. So we were informed by radio and were kept informed about everything that happened in the enclave. We were not only kept informed, but you can also keep track of already our reports, and then from the other side of the enclave you automatically get updates and particularities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you did not see that the fire was targeting civilians. You learned that from someone else by radio; right?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which fire do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that the enclave was under fire from outside. The fire was targeting civilian population. And when I asked you to corroborate that, you said that although you were under cover in a shelter, you received radio information about that. So I'm saying you did not see that the fire targeted civilians. You received information about that.

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The situation you're referring to now, that was prior to the invasion of the enclave, and there was some firing before that too. Again, everything that happened from the north during the fall of the enclave I saw all that, and everything before then, when I was in the bunker, we heard only by radio. So I didn't see that. So that's my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, at one point you said in your statement, the number is 00564816, on page 1, that you were detained at OP Papa on the 14th of July around 8.00 in the morning; right?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. The date is the wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that that's how the statement reads? This is the questionnaire, document number such and such. I stated the number. It's a questionnaire that you filled in. Did you fill in a questionnaire?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made various statements, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that it states here the 14th of July? This is paragraph 9 of this statement.

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see that it reads that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, you were guarded by Serb soldiers at the place where you were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the advance started, we were indeed taken hostage. We were detained, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What do you understand that the definition of hostages is according to you, Mr. Patelski?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I'm deprived of my freedom and I can't walk from A to B and I can't say what I want to say and my equipment is taken from me and I'm held at gunpoint and I'm looking down the barrel of an AK-47, then I think that would be some type of hostage situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you armed? Some weapons were confiscated from you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Some weapons were confiscated at our observation post. We don't carry our arm the entire day. The weapons are kept in a weapon rack, and the moment we were taken hostage, a certain number of colleagues were forced to surrender their arms, and I also had to surrender my arm. And the men who were not on duty, they had their arm in that rack. In the end, we all had to surrender our -- we all had to surrender our arms. We were forced to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see what you said in your statement? Actually, it's also in this questionnaire. On page 2 where you say that you were held, and in the statement that you gave in 2000 and page 3, this is -- actually, let's look at page 2 of the questionnaire first. It's paragraph 11. Taken captive or restricted in your freedom of movement: [In English] [As read] "At that time, we were -- OP Papa north side of the enclave, your access to the enclave through the Papa." [Interpretation] At that point in time was your battalion on the side of the Muslim armed forces? Were they in an alliance and were they helping the Muslim forces? Were you involved in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat that question for me? I didn't follow it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your unit, your battalion, at that time did it place itself on the side of the Muslim army in Srebrenica and get involved in the war?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that I was involved in an incident and a conflict between the Serbs and the Muslims, and all I can say is that I was taken prisoner -- or, rather, I was taken hostage, and everything else is speculation on my part, so I can't make any statement about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what is the difference between a prisoner on a hostage in your opinion? Is there a difference?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why are you asking me that, if you don't mind me asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For the sake of precision, Mr. Patelski. You are describing the situation that you were in as a situation of hostage-taking. This is one criminal act. However, taking captive and holding is something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me -- let us clarify with the Prosecution. Mr. Patelski is not listed as one of the victims of hostage-taking, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: He's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Let us proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You filled in this questionnaire on the 30th of October, 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made various statements, including this one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender the questionnaire, and I would like to also tender the video-clip from 16:30.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please be asked to repeat the counter numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted to say for the record the video-clip which is 40582, that's the 65 ter number, has three parts and the part that Mr. Karadzic played was V000-9035. He started at, I believe, 16:45 to 17:27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you do not objection to the admission of that part?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it part of the Srebrenica trial video?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It is. It's part of 65 ter 40582.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But separate -- irrespective of you're -- the fact that you are tendering that video in its entirety, we'll admit this part for the Defence purpose. Yes. And you have no objection to the admission of his -- his response to this questionnaire?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the video will be Exhibit D2006, and the questionnaire will be Exhibit D2007.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement from 2000, however, this is 00999209, on page 3, you said that you were guarded that whole day. [In English] Guarded all the time that day.

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was this the 14th or the 12th?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And at that time you experienced that as being guarded, and now you are looking at it as being a hostage; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My colleagues and I were placed together in a corner of our observation post and held at gunpoint, so from my perspective that was a hostages situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you didn't say that in 2000. You said that you were being guarded the whole day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this is not a witness to clarify the meaning of "hostage" different from being a prisoner or whatever. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that your camp was not overseen by the Serbian army and that at the time there were Muslim soldiers in the compound; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that -- actually, you said in your statement from 2000, on page 4, that you didn't see anything but that you had the impression that somewhere in the Potocari compound Muslim soldiers were being shot at; is that correct? But you didn't see who was shooting, nor did you see anyone get killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading the piece on the screen right now. Okay. Yes, I remember this part. I can't say who fired those shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you not say that you saw the excavator and that in the compound itself a few people were buried?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about an excavator.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in the debriefing, at your army - this is 0055-7276 to 0055-7277, on page 1 - this is what you said and that the grave was covered, and then you say that it was covered over more. Do you know that to this day there is digging going on, that they are searching for that grave and it's not -- hasn't been found yet, and all of this because somebody at your ministry stated something and misinformed them?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can tell you is what I saw, and if you're referring to the improvised grave in the compound, yes, I did see that. At least I saw it being -- I saw it being shut and the earth being thrown into it. I didn't speak with the person assigned to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me. "I did speak with the person assigned to do that."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was that person? You are saying, thus, that there was a grave dug at the compound and that somebody was buried. Did you see that they were burying somebody in that grave?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat this one more time for you. All I saw was the last moment when the grave was covered. It was basically all finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any bodies in the grave? Whose bodies? How did they die?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose bodies those were and how they died, I don't know. All I saw was part of a hand protruding, and later on that was neatly covered as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Patelski, they're digging there, and they're looking for it there on the basis of your information, and they haven't found anything yet. Was this recorded in your battalion, and who was the person who did that?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who submitted the reports. When I returned from Observation Post Papa, we walked around the base several times to escort and help the different injured and refugees. And once again, I saw a grave being covered there. And how many people they were and which reports were submitted, I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see the grave in the compound in your base, inside the base?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I see what? What's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the grave within the compound, and did your forces deal with it? Under whose jurisdiction was it? Who was digging? Who did the actual burial?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say about this is that we had an engineering commander, and he was responsible for the goings-on within the base. And who assigned the digging of that grave, I can't tell you that. All I can base myself on is what I saw. So I don't know everything surrounding that. All I can tell you is what I saw, and I stand by my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but this was done by UN soldiers, in any case, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What were UN soldiers doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dealing with the grave. They buried somebody there.

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke very briefly with the driver of the excavator, the engineer, and he filled in the grave. When I approached him it was as good as done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any incidents where your equipment at the observation post was being stolen, that Muslims were stealing your equipment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No equipment whatsoever was stolen from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Didn't you say something like that in the debriefing of the 6th of September, 1995, on page 3, about thefts? And that in early June at Papa Post there were threats, that the URFs [as interpreted] would be used against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly what are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that equipment was being stolen at your post? Is it correct what it says here in this statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us upload that statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ERN number is 0134084, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see that? [In English] "The subject knows that in early June, when he was at the OP Papa, on one occasion a threat was made to the effect that the QRF would be used against the Serbs." [Interpretation] We will find the place where you speak about thefts. I think this is at the top of the page. Is what it says here correct? Was it so? Right above this section there is talk about theft; is that right? [In English] "In order to be able to carry out his task. Well, the subject was involved in incidents at the OP Papa a couple of times. On these occasions, the Muslims were stealing at the OP. The subject heard rumours that the colleagues had cocked his weapon on one occasion at the OP during one of the above-mentioned thefts."

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were indeed some moments that thefts were committed, yes, by the Muslims. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And do you know that the Serb side was always afraid that one day your weapons will end up in Muslim hands and that they would use them against us?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at page 2 of the debriefing, please. Did you order, did you give instructions for the grave to be dug up, and were there not some six bodies involved?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which grave do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which grave was it that you gave instructions to be dug up and to have six bodies placed there?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand this question. I don't know what you're looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will tell you that you stated that you saw or you had six bodies that needed to be buried behind the compound in Potocari, that you issued instructions for a large grave to be dug up, 2 metres long, where these six victims could be buried. And those victims were buried, a new-born that died with its umbilical cord still around its neck, then a 78-year-old man, a 16-year-old girl who died from diabetes, and two others. There is no information as to the reason why they died. Did this happen?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we just have the correct cite? I don't see it on the page. I'm not sure from where we ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before doing that, do you remember such statement, Mr. Patelski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know anything about that. And I'm not sure exactly what you said, but I certainly didn't issue any such instructions. At the time I was a soldier. I didn't issue instructions. I carried them out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] [Indiscernible] Dealt with the funeral proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm asking you to upload that statement. This is not it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the debriefing of the Royal Netherlands Army, ERN 1088132. I thought it was the same briefing. There aren't two. I was thinking of the 1D number. I thought that there was only one debriefing. The ERN number 108832 [as interpreted]. And then this would be on page 2. [In English] R1088132, R. [Indiscernible], R.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, would you need some time for your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I will need a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the separation of men, and you said that at least 100 Muslims were separate, men, Muslim men, were separated and transported. How many buses is that, one or two?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not going to make a statement about that. I'm not going to estimate how many people fit into a bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that in 2000 you said that about 100 men were separated?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's perfectly conceivable that I said that in 2000. There were quite a few men, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Patelski. Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic asked you about D2007. May we have that, please. It's the questionnaire from October of 1995, and on the first page he asked you about the date that you were held -- held captive in OP Papa. Now, today you testified that that took place on the 12th, but when you did this questionnaire in October of 1995, and we're looking specifically at number 9, you answered that it was on the 14th. Is it possible that you could have gotten the date wrong when you said on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we show --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's a bit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why we don't show him page 7, which he wrote in Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see 14 July on the screen. Conceivably I made a mistake about the date. It's been a while, and I had to think way back about everything that I had seen and what the date had been, but the fact is that it's known on what date the enclave fell. And once again exactly which date, it could have been the 14th or the 12th, I can't say, but the facts are as they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 22446. Mr. Patelski, today you were asked about sniping, and you were asked about the distance the snipers were from both your post and from the Muslim houses, and on page 3 today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm receiving Dutch interpretation, but I'm not sure that your microphone has been activated. Mr. Harvey does not hear it. Do you hear my voice?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: It has just come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And on page 3 of today's daily transcript, Mr. Karadzic remarked the distance was far too great and that it did not happen, and on page 12 he said there is no such thing in the UN reports, although it happened if we are to believe you. Now we're going to look at 22446. This is your statement that you gave to the OTP in June of 2000. We're going to go to page 2. Do you remember being interviewed by the OTP in 2000?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether that was the OTP. Yes, several -- I was asked several questions at that time, but do you mean questions concerning the snipers?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My first question is: Do you remember being interviewed by somebody in 2000 and this report being produced?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I was here as well to make a statement in 2000, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And we're going to look at paragraph 4 and see what you said about sniping in 2000, and there, the end of that paragraph, it says: "Two weeks before the fall of the enclave, I saw two Serbian tanks moving close to that house. I saw that the snipers were posted on the surrounding hills and the artillery and mortars firing in the direction of the enclave." Sir, do you remember making that statement back in 2000?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's entirely correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 2095, please. We're going to look at a few pages of this, but the first page of this indicates that it's a report from July 4th. It's a Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade report. Now, if we can go to the page ending in 6541, please. And the bottom of 6541, it says page 9 in the English. I think we have the wrong page there. Apologies if that's my fault. The ERN ends in 6541, and the top says "Inventory of Ammunition." Your Honour, it appears that the B/C/S is probably right. I just don't think the English is right. At least that's first -- okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.text: My name is Robert Franken.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If I may read a summary, please. Colonel Robert Franken served in the Royal Netherlands Army in various command and staff positions. He retired after 33 years of service with the rank of colonel. From January 1995 to July 1995, he was assigned to DutchBat Battalion 3 in Potocari. During this time he held the position of major and deputy commander officer. His immediate superior was DutchBat commander Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans. As DCO, Franken was responsible for organising supplies to keep the battalion operational. In early 1995, the VRS began to place increasingly strict restrictions on the passage of supply convoys to the Srebrenica enclave. VRS approval was required for both the contents and number of trucks in every convoy. The VRS categorically denied supplies relating to weapons systems, spare parts, testing devices, ammunition, and communication equipment. VRS restrictions on convoys increased after February when the last fuel convoy was approved. UNHCR convoys were subject to the same approval process and restrictions. And the colonel has described the collective VRS convoy restrictions as a convoy terror. The restriction had a significant impact on DutchBat's ability to carry out its mission. Due to lack of fuel, DutchBat personnel had to patrol the enclave on foot and chop wood for heat. They could not keep their medical station operation and were unable to purify water or cook food. The VRS convoy restrictions also reduced the DutchBat weapons and ammunition supplies and prevented proper maintenance of those weapons. DutchBat rotations were also affected. When Franken arrived in Potocari, the battalion strength was over 300. By July 1995, only 147 combat-trained soldiers remained. The VRS began to increase its attack on DutchBat patrols and observation points from April 1995 onwards. Franken has described the June 3rd attack on OP Echo as a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please read more slowly for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me. Franken described the June 3rd attack on OP Echo as a test case for future attacks. During that attack, 40 Serb infantry supported by a T55 battle tank forced the peacekeepers out of the OP after firing on it and striking its observation post -- excuse me, tower. On July 6, there's the attack on the enclave including direct VRS firing on OPs, shelling on the town, firing on Potocari and its surroundings. This attack resulted in significant civilian casualties. Between the 6th and 10th of July, the colonel received reports of further attacks by the VRS on various OPs. On July 9th, the colonel was ordered to form blocking positions with APCs in order to prevent further VRS penetration into the safe area and to force the VRS to stay static enough to be struck by close-air support. These APCs also came under direct VRS tank and artillery fire resulting in one APCs being shot off the road and shrapnel wounds and injuries to DutchBat peacekeepers. The recovery vehicle sent to retrieve the APC came under fire and had to withdraw. On the 10th, the colonel's blocking positions came under fire and there was massive shelling of Srebrenica including the UN Bravo Company resulting in further injuries to civilians and DutchBat personnel. The VRS issued an ultimatum to civilians. BiH soldiers, DutchBat, and UNHCR to leave by 6.00 -- 600 hours on July 11th. The UNPROFOR responded with an ultimatum of its own that the VRS should withdraw to the so-called Morillon line by 6.00 in the morning or there would be massive air-strikes. On the 11th of July, the colonel received reports about the fall of the remaining OPs. The DutchBat soldiers manning these OPs were made to hand in their small-calibre weapons and were taken to Bratunac where they were held prisoner by the VRS. In the meantime, the civilian population of the enclave were fleeing in great numbers from Srebrenica to Potocari. Bravo Company peacekeepers accompanied the refugees, and Franken received reports of shelling of the column. Bravo Company picked up the wounded and transported them to Potocari. Franken made sure that the peacekeepers guided the refugees to the back of the Potocari compound and away from the road as he believed that the VRS would fire on them. Refugees were also directed to abandoned factories and bus stations. Close-air support was first delivered in the afternoon of July 11th and Franken received a threat that if air support continued, the VRS would shell the compound housing the refugees and would kill the soldiers in Bratunac. Franken took the threat to shell the compound seriously, because the Serb forces had fired on refugees with all their means before. Shortly following the threat, there was a mortar shelling of the area of the bus station and a full round of the multiple rocket system in the area of Potocari. The shelling caused injury to some refugees and instilled fear in the population. Franken observed that the refugees were totally exhausted and in bad condition. It was if the world had stopped for them. On the morning of the 12th, Franken observed Serb forces advancing towards Potocari from the north. Sometime after noon, a large number of buses and trucks began arriving. Franken was ordered to co-ordinate support for the evacuation of the refugees. That day, he met with the VRS colonel, Acamovic, who identified himself as logistics officer. He also met with a VRS colonel, Jankovic, who identified himself as being from Pale and said his mission was to co-ordinate DutchBat's withdrawal. Franken was told by Jankovic that the Serb forces already had 6.000 POWs. Franken also estimated that there were approximately 1.000 men being held in the compound in the surrounding area. In total, he states that there appears to have been up to 7.000 men involved in the events of mid-July, 1995. Franken ordered Major Boering, and a captain to escort the first convoy. Franken believed that although the refugees left voluntarily, they had been subjected to humanitarian crisis that left them no alternative but to get on the buses. He received reports that the first and second convoys went well, but thereafter the VRS stopped all of the UN escorts and stripped them of their weapons, equipment, and clothing. Franken believed the Serb forces did not want the UN escorts to be witnesses and wanted them out of the way. He complained to Jankovic to no avail. General Mladic had announced that the men were to be separated from the group of refugees to determine if they were war criminals. After the first convoy, men were separated from the group immediately after they left the perimeter secured by the peacekeepers. They were taken to the white house for interrogation and then transported in the direction of Bratunac -- Bratunac. The men were forced to leave their personal belongings in front of the white house in a large pile which the Serb forces later burned. The Serbs consistently thwarted efforts to have UN officials escort the buses and also prevented peacekeepers from investigating reports of maltreatment of the men in the white house. Franken complained to Jankovic about the situation but nothing changed. He attempted to register the Muslim men, compiling at one stage a list of over 200 men. He informed Jankovic that he had done so, but he did not hand over the list. Between the 12th and the 13th of July, he received reports of executions of Muslim men. One of his OP crews also reported seeing a large group of men kneeling on a soccer field next to a road in rows with their hands on their necks. Jankovic had contacted Franken to arrange a truck to bring that OP crew back and during this time the conditions of the refugees on the DutchBat base were rapidly deteriorating. Franken recalls that at least 11 people died from wounds, dehydration and exhaustion. After the general population moved out, there were still 59 wounded Muslims remaining. The Serbs wanted to keep them in Serb territory. Franken contacted the ICRC and MSF to evacuate them. On the 17th of July, Jankovic led a Serb delegation which included Momir Nikolic to arrange the evacuation. On that same day, Jankovic asked Franken and a Muslim -- the Muslim representative, Nesib Mandic, to sign a declaration. The declaration stated that the evacuations had been conducted in accordance with international law and the Geneva Conventions. Colonel Franken stated that that part of the document stating that the population could remain in the enclave was nonsense since they never had a realistic opportunity to stay. He stated that being as afraid and lethargic as the refugees were, staying was not a choice. Franken signed the declaration because Jankovic had indicated that doing so would facilitate the evacuation of the wounded. On the 21st of July, Franken left Potocari with some of his troops. He observed General Nikolai, General Mladic, and Colonel Karremans saluting the units as they passed by. Colonel Franken drove off.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you a few questions.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry, but before you do so, it's very kind of you to promote me to colonel, but I was -- I retired as a lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction, sir. I'm going to ask you some questions on a number of convoy documents that you've seen before. And if I can ask for the assistance of the usher. I'm giving these to you in hard copy so it might be easier, but they'll also come up on the screen. If we may have 65 ter 19005, please. Sir, this is a document dated January 31st, 1995. It's entitled "Principles for Freedom of Movement." And it regards -- have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, but not when I was in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's fine. I just want to ask you a couple things about it. Under number 2, it indicates that: "UNPROFOR will notify the Serb army authorities 48 hours in advance of convoy movements and 24 hours for single vehicles." Was that your experience at the time? Were you required to give advance notice.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: We had to give advance notice 72 hours before to BH command. So that helps with what's stated here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And under C, it says: "Approval for convoy movement will be given by the Serbian army HQ. In case of disapproval of a convoy, the Serbian authority is obliged to give a proper explanation, stating the reasons of refusal of a particular convoy." And, Mr. Franken, is that what actually happened? Did UNPROFOR receive proper explanations for refusals?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, I do not know of that because I was not a party in that communication. I asked for a convoy and then BH command applied for it at the Serb authorities, so when they refused then the communication due to that, I never saw that or heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And under paragraph 3 "Control": "Convoys may be checked only once by an SA check-points." To your knowledge, were convoys checked only once or more than once?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: More than once. As far as I reflect, at least three times.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes that will be accepted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4186, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to look at 65 ter 3521, please. This is a document from March 10th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, as I go through these documents it's going to go chronologically. So we're now on March 10th. This is a Main Staff document to the Drina Corps, and it's one that regards whether the UNPROFOR convoys have been approved or not. If we can go to paragraph -- excuse me, page 3. And on page 3 there's a note. This regards a convoy for Srebrenica. It says: "We did not allow the following three" -- there's a question as to fuel tankers and five trailer trucks "... from Srebrenica the same vehicles and a jeep and 28 personnel members. Colonel Franken can you tell us the last time the enclave received fuel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That was in February, end of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this document is March 10th. In the month of March, do you have any memory of receiving fuel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, we did not receive any fuel as of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If you go further down on that page under "no" it says: "We did not allow 36 metres cubed of diesel fuel." Is it consistent with your memory that -- strike that: "We did not allow 36 metres cubed of diesel fuel and additional ten crates of dry food, additional five crates of frozen foot, additional ten crates of cold food?" Can you tell us what the food situation was like in the middle of March?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, we did not have any fresh food so we lived on combat rations still in stock at our compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we go to the last page of this document. It's the last paragraph. Pardon me. It's the second to last page in the English. It's the last page. It says: "Discuss the information on unapproved convoys with check-points. Do not tell third persons and do not give any explanation to UNPROFOR representatives (pretend you did for the get them). If a convoy shows up at a crossing point, return it to the place of departure." Do you know if your convoy drivers ever got any explanations as to the refusals?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. Convoy drivers didn't nor their convoy commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit P4187.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: 65 ter 3522. This is again March 10th. It's a Main Staff document to the Drina Corps. We're going to look at page 2 of the English. And it says: "... importing of fuel is forbidden. We are expecting that in spite of the information on restrictions we forwarded to the co-ordinating body for humanitarian aid that UNHCR will try to take fuel to the enclave. It should be prevented." Mr. Franken, can you tell me, as a result of fuel being forbidden, what was the effect of that on the everyday activity of DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, as I came there in January, the fuel stocks were very low in the beginning. So we had very little fuel, which meant that we were not able to rise any energy, because all the energy we had came from generators. We were not able to heat. In the end, we were not able to cook and so on. We had to do everything on foot, even resupplying our OPs. For that occasion, we occasionally used local ponies to bring stuff up to the OPs observation post. So, in general, that is the situation and consequence of this, as I call it, convoy terror.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4188, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Look at 65 ter 21661, and this is a multiple page document. It's dated March 31st. It's a Main Staff document and it's to the UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo. At the end of this document appear to be requested from UNPROFOR for convoys. Sir, can you tell us what the process was by which UNPROFOR requested convoys to come to the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as I know, it went like this: I had a need for certain supplies. I communicated that to my logistic command, Dutch logistic command which was in Bosnia-Herzegovina area, and they came up with requests to BiH command for a convoy. They -- they -- destined [sic] what cars, how many cars, et cetera, et cetera, and the amounts and the exact sort, et cetera, so the contents. That goes to BH command, and from BH command there goes a request to the Serb -- Muslim Serb staff and then they or not consented it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I know you've looked at this document before and there are requests at the end of it, and at the first page it says at 12, 13, and 14 that these requests to Srebrenica were denied. Is this an example of the process by which you just spoke about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, the only thing I -- because I did not get this kind of information in the enclave. The only result of the procedure was that I heard that the convoy wouldn't come because the Serbs denied it. The exact text and -- of denials or the request done by BH command I never saw those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I only heard the result and that was mostly no.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the results recorded here 12, 13, and 14 are those consistent with your memory?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I would ask for this admission, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4189, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 3664, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is April 2nd. It's a Main Staff document to the Drina Corps, and in this document, up in the right-hand corner, there's handwriting, and it says: "Not a single convoy or ICRC or Doctors Without Borders may enter Srebrenica without my permission and presence." And it's signed by M. Nikolic. Sir, in the beginning of April -- first, let me ask you this: Mr. Nikolic, do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I suppose that is the captain or Major Nikolic we knew as being a member of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And were there discussions between Nikolic and your liaison officers about convoy needs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, because we supposed Nikolic was not in a level in that decision-making.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: After the beginning of April - this is April 2nd - did you see any ICRC or MSF convoys coming through?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not as I recollect. Later in May, as I recollect, there was one, I believe, MSF transport. But when I'm correct that was personnel, not stocks.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So in the month of April you did not see [overlapping speakers] convoys?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would ask for admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4190, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you know where this was seized?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can have a moment to get that information, I will get it for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking because this is a Main Staff document addressed to Drina Corps and somebody wrote it at Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, during this spring of 1995, did you ever take leave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I was on a leave in March.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And for how long was your leave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Ten days.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And did Colonel Karremans ever take leave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. When I came back Colonel Karremans went on leave, so he returned somewhere halfway down April or in the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we may have 65 ter 22012.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: These are three documents dated May 18th, and if we can look at the last page of the English. This is to General Mladic from Janvier. And in the last paragraph it says: "For the past three weeks we have been attempting to effect the normal and scheduled rotation of personnel from our peacekeeping forces in Srebrenica, and, at present, there are approximately 170 soldiers waiting in Zagreb who have been unable to take up their responsibilities due to restrictions of movement imposed by your forces. Included in this is a total of a 13-member DutchBat medical team required for the medical support of our UN forces in Srebrenica. Almost daily since the 27th of April, there have been refusals from your authorities to allow clearance for these rotations ... I believe you would agree with me that the situation is not acceptable and only serves to heighten tension at a critical period." Sir, can you tell us whether this last paragraph we've just reviewed was consistent with what was going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask for the admission of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit P4191.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is an UNPROFOR headquarter Weekly Situation Report. It's dated the 29th of May to 4 June of 1995, and if we may go to the fifth page of the English, please. It's paragraph 17. "Situation in the enclaves": "Limited amounts of humanitarian assistance through convoys reached Tuzla during the reporting period. All the other enclaves did not receive their scheduled supplies. Should the present state of affairs persist, the enclaves which depend entirely on humanitarian assistance will suffer tremendously." Does this describe the humanitarian aid situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Completely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And to what extent were civilians already suffering by May?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, the only food that was present in -- in the enclave for the civilians was stocks or that what they -- what do you call that? Made themselves the little lambs, a bit of vegetables that's -- things like that. But it was absolutely insufficient food for the civil population.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
