utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask for admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Exhibit P4192.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Certificate 03706, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is a June 15th document. It's a Main Staff to the Drina Corps, and if I can go to the third page of the English, please. Here it says: "Check the level of fuel in tanks. Have the necessary tool, a stick, ready for the checking. Measure the level of fuel in the tanks at the entrance of the enclave and after. Carry out the checking and enable them to move along the above-cited routes." To what does this paragraph refer in regard to this checking?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Probably the -- the -- the strict control they want to have on -- on the fuel levels, fuel stock levels, within the enclave, because they want to check whether they did not get some fuel out of the tanks of the vehicles coming in and that the use of fuel was just because the struck itself drove and we didn't take anything out just to stock up our fuels -- fuel reserves, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So the necessary tool to which it refers is actually going into the tank of the convoy truck?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask for its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4193, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And now 65 ter 3488, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is June 18th. It's a Main Staff document. Look at paragraph 3 in English where it says: "Cargo for Srebrenica: One container with eight pallets of frozen food, one container with eight pallets of dry food, and one tanker with 11 cubic metres of diesel fuel." And a little bit down, it says again: "I demand a detailed check of all vehicles, including the inspection of cargo. Pay special attention to the fuel in the fuel tanks and the fuel being brought into the enclave." Sir, can you comment on the parts that I just read? First of all, what was the food situation like? This is 18th of June.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Somewhere in that area, we were through our own supplies as well. We didn't have any combat rations as well, so we ate about ten days for breakfast peanut butter and rice; for lunch, rice and peanut butter; and for variation, for dinner, peanut butter and rice. So there was not much food for us as well. I recollect that, indeed, a convoy came in, a couple of vehicles, with some combat rations. I can't recollect whether it was exactly the 18th or 19th or something, but I do not recollect fuel coming in.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And again, this speaks a little bit further down about the detailed check of all vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Is that what you spoke about a little earlier?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I move for admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4194, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly make a pause between questions and answers, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is to General Delic from Nikolai. And in the middle of this document, the paragraph beginning with "Although." This is talking about DutchBat: "Although this unit has been suffering a lack of fuel for several months now, it still occupies its OPs along the confrontation line and is still by its presence contributes to the protection of the civilian population living in the area. I have to admit that the lack of fuel prevents them from conducting mechanised patrols and that due to security measures they also stopped their foot patrols temporarily." Can you tell us about foot patrols and how the foot patrols came about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: First a remark. We never stopped our foot patrols, so I don't know where this comes from. Well, it meant that we -- in the average, we had ten up to -- yeah, around ten foot patrols in the area between the observation posts, which meant that they had combat load and had to do patrols over about 10, 15 kilometres in accidented [phoen] -- or in hillious terrain. Well -- is that an answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And where it says: "The unit has been suffering a lack of fuel for several months now..."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, we move for admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4195, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is the same date, June 26th, and one's to Mladic, Nikolai. And in the middle the first paragraphs, it says: "As you are very well aware, my troops are limited in their ability to execute effective patrolling as a direct result of the lack of fuel." Again, this is similar to the document we just saw. Was this consistent with what happened at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It is consistent. At that time, we were not allowed to do foot patrols as well in Bosnian Serb area. I suggested that to Nikolic once when he reported an attack north of the enclave, and said, Okay, let us patrol down there and see what happens and see whether we can find the route the ABiH took. But it was not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4196, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is July 1. Go to page 3 of the English. It's a Main Staff document. On page 3 of the English it's -- there's a note. And it's talking about the movement of convoys under 5 and 6, and this was personnel movement, which has been approved conditionally, should be specially controlled by teams at check points and liaison officers of the Drina Corps. Sir, can you tell us about the rotation of personnel in and out of the enclave and what was happening with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, in general, the rotations stopped half April. That's why we had 170 guys in Zagreb, and this is probably concerning the rotation of my medical staff. We had some surgeons who were due to rotate, and that is what this is about. We were not allowed to rotate completely as I recollect. About ten guys of that ration couldn't go along.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So for July 1 this rotation does not include combat transport?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. It's a personnel rotation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4197, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm looking for the second page in English. This is July 6th. This is a BiH combat report. We're going to go to paragraph 3, the last part of paragraph 3, "This morning," it says: "This morning I was told by the UN liaison officer that 25 UN members left Srebrenica and that as many were supposed to have arrived along with a number of officers from the command of the new battalion. However, the Serbs in Zvornik let in only 20 UN members through, mostly medical and administrative personnel." So when you commented earlier about your medical staff rotation does this refer to that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And under number 4: "Situation continues to be exceptionally difficult. The food convoy announced for today has not arrived. Elderly and weak persons are in an exceptionally difficult situation due to starvation. The first people to die of hunger in the area of Srebrenica after the demilitarisation were registered today. I request that every effort be made to deliver food to our area." Sir, were you aware of people dying in the area due hunger in the beginning of July?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, and, as I recollect, the first reports came to me around the 20th of June. So one or two weeks earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask for the admission of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Exhibit P4198.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, we're now going to move on to the attack, and first I'd like to talk to you about OP Echo which happened on June 3rd, and in your statement it's paragraph 44. You refer to it as a test case.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Why did you refer to it as a test case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: If you are a military unit and you are attacked, you try to find out why and what the purpose of that attack is. So at the beginning, I thought it was a beginning of an offensive to go for Srebrenica, the city itself, and it proved out that they didn't advance, although they were successful, which is strange because a military unit that attacks -- tries to keep up his speed and attack when he is successful, but they stopped. I then sent down what later became Observation Post Sierra and Uniform, and I was surprised that they could come down south that far. They came to the very edge of the Zeleni Jadar valley which meant that the Serbs, in fact, did, more or less, retire from their utmost deepness of the attack, so they were on the high edge, and that obviously withdraw from there to the factory again. Then, I concluded that it must have been a test case: First to see what would be the reaction of -- of UNPROFOR, DutchBat specifically. Would they stand in their OP or would they leave on request, which we did not; and then triggered by their withdrawal to the factory again, see whether UNPROFOR would react with air support because the conditions for giving air support were fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you ask for air support?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Did you get it? No. That's why I concluded it's a test case. The Serbs want to see how UNPROFOR reacts on an attack on -- on a UN unit and crossing the UN -- the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 3852.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is a June 2nd document. It's a Drina Corps document. This is the day before OP Echo fell. This is an order from Milenko Zivanovic. Sir, have you looked at this order before?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. Well, I've seen it here, but not of course in the period I was in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is an order under number 1. It says: "He shall order him the following:" And then there's a whole list of very specific items. Mr. Franken, is there anything unusual -- unusual about this document to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, it's very detailed. To make clear what I mean, for us an attack on a location as OP Echo would be -- well, almost a platoon action when not a company action, and the way it is done is left to the company commander. There is not a higher command interfering with this. And here I see that a corps level interferes with incredible details, and not even that, sending down some officers to control the -- the attack or even to command the attack. That's, in my military mind, very unusual.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I know you've had an opportunity to go through all these details, but is this document consistent with what actually happened the following day when OP Echo was taken?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It's consistent with the reports I got, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I would ask for the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4199, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if we can have 65 ter 22815, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, this is a document from June 3rd, 1900 hours, so that evening. It's a VRS combat report. And under number 1, it says: "After a successful operation and the forceful expulsion of the UNPROFOR from the Zeleni Jadar post ..." The Zeleni Jadar post, is that OP Echo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: "... the enemy was observed systematically building up large forces and moving them from the Srebrenica sector towards the general sector of Zeleni Jadar. Their formation included two armoured personnel carriers and one tank." Just if we can go down a little bit further to the next paragraph: "The inhabitants of Zeleni Jadar moved out in panic following UNPROFOR's withdrawal and large groups of people (probably civilians) were observed in the afternoon moving towards Srebrenica." Is this consistent with what happened after OP Echo fell?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: First, the reaction on those two personnel carriers and one tank, to my knowledge, there were no armoured personnel carriers and tank on the Bosnia side. Remember that in that area my observe posts Sierra and Uniform were established and when there were tanks operating in that area it would have been reported to me, so I doubt that observation. Secondly, as they mean Zeleni Jadar, as I know it, there were no inhabitants of Zeleni Jadar because that was absolutely left. It was on -- exactly on the confrontation line. So it's a bit puzzling to me. If they mean the population of the Swedish Shelter Project, possible that they were starting to flee in the direction of Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: -- which is consistent with Post Pusmulici because that is a village quite close to that shelter project.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. That was exactly what I was going to ask you. The next paragraph is: "The general conclusion is that the enemy was taken completely by surprise. They did not have full or permanent control of their forward defence and they seemed quite disorganised." Is this consistent with your memory as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as the ABiH is concerned, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And on the second page, before paragraph 3, it says: "The men are rather tired. A strong police check-point is expected to arrive in Zeleni Jadar." And then under 4, it says: "Ensure the arrival of police to man the check-point in Zeleni Jadar as soon as possible." Sir, can you tell us what was your -- what's your memory as to the presence of police in the area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: We were not aware of a police check-point at Zeleni Jadar. Probably it was out of our line of sight, but they -- they -- how do you say that? Later on, we saw many times that police forces were integrated in the operations of the BSA, the regular forces. So it's not -- to me, it's not a surprise that they did that at Zeleni Jadar as well, but again we did not observe that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4200, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're going to play two videos at this -- at this point. And again, as you know, that's 65 ter 40582. The companion transcript, the book, is 65 ter 03099. And at this point, we -- we have shown a number of these videos, as you know, with the witnesses, and we would ask for the full admission of the video. I spoke to Mr. Robinson before to see his comment on our request, and he has no objection as I understand it. I would also pointed out that in the book itself, the back of the book it lists the entire video and it gives the sources, and so for the ease of continuing on with the video and the book I would ask for the admission of both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We think that by the time we've heard the testimony of Mr. Ruez, in particular, that there would be an established foundation for the admission of the video, so it seems easier to admit it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Together with the book itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit them and give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the video will be Exhibit P4201 and the accompanying book will be Exhibit P4202.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. So we'll now play P4201. This is going to be the video ending in 9014. We're starting at minute 15. And in regard to the transcript, if you care to look at that, at P4202, it's e-court pages 197 to 198.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By any chance do you have the hard copy page numbers? Last four digits.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That is 7815. And just to tell you that this part of the video are trucks coming into Potocari, and there's actually not a lot of speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, we just saw a number of people coming off of trucks. It appears to be a facility. Can you tell us -- can you identify this area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. It's the HQ of DutchBat at Potocari, and the building you see is an industrial hall which -- in which we later had about 5- or 6.000 refugees sheltered, and these are transports coming in from the Srebrenica area.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And were you there when this was happening?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I saw this myself, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We'll continue to play the video, and it's going to change over to a part of the video with Mladic entering the town of Srebrenica. And for the Trial Chamber, for the transcript, this is 7815. And the time-code where we just stopped was 18 minutes and 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, could you recognise that tank?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. It's an APCs of DutchBat, and seeing the number, it is the APCs of Captain Hageman who was fired upon by a Serb tank when he tried to reach Bravo 2, one of the blocking positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is this the tank you refer to in your statement at paragraph 53?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I suppose it's 52, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: For the record that's 18 minutes and 59 seconds and we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Just stopped at 19 minutes and 59 seconds, right after the person says, "Do not paint over it."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, were there occasions where your equipment was stolen?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The question is whether there were occasions when my equipment was stolen. Yes, many of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll continue on, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And here we're at 21 minutes and 11 seconds, and General Mladic has just said: "Put that on so it can be seen that you are an UNPROFOR member."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, if you know, to what is he referring?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Probably he wants to use that APCs with a UN-looking crew for anything. I had reports later on that -- that infantry, Serb infantry, used stolen UN equipment like flak jackets and helmets to pose as DutchBat members.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to show you another part of the video now. This is -- again it's P4201 and it's V000-9016, and we're going to start at 11 minutes and 20 seconds. We'll go to 17 minutes and 45 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We've stopped the video at 17 minutes and 45 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, can you describe the vantage point from where that video was taken?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, as I can see it, it's from the tower which was on the building in which our HQ was, within our compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in which direction were those buses moving?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: In the direction of Bratunac, and the departure point is right in front of our main gate.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if you know, what was the day and the time of that video?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As I see it, I suggest it's the 13th, the last day of the -- of the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I have no more questions for you. Mr. President, for the record, you had asked for where we found P4190. It was the document with the handwriting of Momir Nikolic. That was seized by the ICTY at the Bratunac Brigade on March 6, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break, Mr. Franken, for an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For an hour, and we'll resume at 1.35, but there's one matter, albeit briefly, to deal with in your absence confidentially, so if you could excuse yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break for an hour. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.36 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Franken, as you heard that your evidence in other cases as well as the statements were admitted in the form of amalgamated statements in lieu of your examination-in-chief, you will be further asked by Mr. Karadzic in his cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Franken. If you don't mind, I would prefer addressing you as Mr. So-and-so, rather than Lieutenant-Colonel So-and-so because it's quite long in our language at least.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what I'd like to ask you: How did you understand that restriction regarding fuel? Why did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: If you control the logistic support of an isolated unit like DutchBat III was, you can control his operational capability, and, in my opinion, the aim of that convoy terror, as I call it, was to diminish that capability of DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why would the DutchBat bother us? Why would we want to diminish the capability of DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, it's not a question for me. Probably you could better ask that question to the ones that did diminish our logistical situation. You could analyse that if the Serbs wanted a solution for the enclaves, for instance, an attack neutralising it, it would be in their interest to have the operational capacities of DutchBat diminished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why would we be bothered by DutchBat? Do you think that we expected you to fight against us? Your mandate was not to defend the enclave, was it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, again you asked me a question why you or you said "we," do anything or what the reasons were for your own action. I do not know. I can only say that the logistic situation was that -- that way that we were not capable to, if necessary, deploy our operational capability.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What would your task be for which you would require operational capability? What was it that you did? Did you demilitarised the zone?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: First question was: What was it that we did. According to our orders, we deterred by presence, so to say; second question: Whether I did demilitarise the zone, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were trying to deter clashes whereby Serbs did not attack until the month of July. Did you manage to deter incursions by Oric's force into Serb-held territory? Did you manage to deter the killing of Serbs, the torching of villages?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: First, the Serbs did attack before July. I consider the attack on OP Echo as a Serb attack and that was in June. Secondly, the second question is we were not able to withhold the 28th Division of actions into Serb territory. That is correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to say to you that we had expected you to demilitarise the zone, prevent the 28th Division from killing us, then this is what I put to you: It was in our interest for you to have operational capability. Wouldn't that be logical?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, it would have been logical only that the convoy terror indicates the opposite. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, this thinking of yours, these conclusions of yours regarding the reasons for restrictions, would that be the one and only explanation or can there be another explanation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, to me it's the -- the only explanation, as I thought of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tomorrow we'll probably show that, but would you agree that there were cases of smuggling, not by a unit or its command but by individuals from the UN force? The smuggling primarily of fuel, ammunition, and so on.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I heard of that, but as far as I know, it did not happen in the case of DutchBat III and the enclave of Srebrenica concerning the battalion itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What do you say to -- I think, Mr. Franken, that you can just lean back and then the microphone problem will be resolved. You are too close to the microphone -- or, rather, you were too close to the microphone. And what do you say to this, Mr. Franken: If this did not happen for the reasons that you mentioned, that were your conclusion -- rather, if reports were received from the ground that convoys were being abused and that there were convoys that smuggled fuel, would you understand that that was the reason, then, rather than any intention of taking the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Again, I'm not aware of facts of convoys coming into Srebrenica for the battalion were abused. Then again, I can't imagine that you would say we won't bring in fuel or smuggle fuel, because when you wanted us -- what the hell?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are being asked by the interpreter to speak to the microphone, but I hope there will work again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Otherwise I will stand up and speak louder, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, there couldn't have been the question of smuggling fuel. The thing was, we needed fuel, and bringing in fuel authorised by everybody would have solved a lot of problems. So I can't react on smuggling fuel. Then again, as far as UN convoys to Srebrenica DutchBat III are concerned, there was no abusing of those convoys. I'm pretty sure of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation as to how come the 28th Division had fuel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Old stores or perhaps smuggled in through Zepa. I do not know, but it is just possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How come there's fuel in Zepa? Zepa's an enclave as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Again, it was just an idea that could have come from Zepa. I do not know about that. It's a possibility, and I'm not aware of the logistic situation in Zepa in those times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that if you had this document that I will show now, you would have taken this possibility into account as well. This is what I put to you: The Main Staff did not act in that direction out of any kind of ill-intention but, rather, because they had been warned from the ground that there was smuggling of fuel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show Mr. Franken D157. Could I please have the translation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have the Serbian version, and you can see the English version. On the 12th of May, 1995, the command of the Birac brigade is informing the corps command and then the corps command, of course, is forwarding this information to the Main Staff and you can read it for yourself. There's no need for me to read it out. UNPROFOR, UNHCR, and other international organisations have been transporting fuel illegally to Muslims in the enclaves of Sarajevo, Gorazde, Zepa, and Srebrenica. And then there's a description here as to how this was actually done. Were you aware of this report from the field?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, I never read that report because I was not in the line of communication of this organisation. That's one. But again, why are we speaking of smuggling of fuel? There is an enclave, there is a Dutch Battalion, there is a civilian enclave who needs to survive fuel, so why just don't let the fuel in? I don't understand this smuggling. Obviously when you say smuggling you did not have the intention to kept them -- to let them have fuel. So again, this document is not known to me, and again, I'm not aware. I was not reported, and I'm pretty firm about not abusing the UN convoys into Srebrenica for, in this case, DutchBat III.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this is how this was smuggling. A lot of fuel comes in, and you leave with a minimal quantity, and you leave this fuel to our enemies. Had Srebrenica been demilitarised, everything would have been easier for the population, for us. However, do you remember that after each convoy came, the Muslim army, both in Gorazde and in Srebrenica, the 28th Division, that is, were a lot more active in their offensives?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see after a convoy -- well, first, you say we left fuel to your enemy. That is incorrect. I never gave the 28th Division any amount of fuel. Whether or not there was smuggling of fuel within UNHCR convoys, I do not know of, and I'm not responsible for that. So we had no reports that was more active -- more activities in their offensives after a UN convoy, being a convoy meant for DutchBat, came in. That is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I kindly ask you not to feel attacked. When I say "you," I'm referring to someone from the UN. I'm confident that not a single officer did that. However, it did happen, and you know that yourself, that individuals were involved in this kind of trade, smuggling. They sold things to the option, bought other things from the population, and so on. Were there not such cases?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, before the last question everything in in front of it was a statement. It's argumentative, it's a waste of time, and this witness deserves better than this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I had just wanted to apologise to you, Mr. Franken. When I say "you," I'm not referring to you personally or the institution of the United Nations. I'm meaning individuals from the UN. I'm not attacking a single officer. That was the statement I had to make. However, were you aware that certain individuals were involved in unlawful activity, certain individuals who were members of the UN force?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, I did not feel attacked, and if you say "you" to me I think you mean DutchBat, and that's why I reacted. Whether there were members of UN organisations that did smuggle, I do not know of that. I can only confirm that it was not done by members of DutchBat or my logistic command coming in with logistic convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you accept that I'm not specifically referring to the Dutch Battalion? Quite simply, I'm referring to the presence of the international community and its representatives because it doesn't only say UNPROFOR and UNHCR here, it also says other international organisations. So I'm absolutely not accusing your battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, he answered did he not know of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franken, do you agree that regardless of whether that is correct or not, the Main Staff received information from the ground to the effect that this kind of thing was happening? Do you agree that these were sufficient grounds for the Main Staff to exercise caution and impose restrictions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Whether the Main Staff got information and how valuable and trustworthy that information was, I just read that report. I did not know of that in that time, and it's not -- to me, it's not that relevant. Whether there were sufficient grounds to exercise caution, yeah, perhaps, but the restrictions again, I do not understand why you speak of smuggling fuel if the fuel is meant for an enclave, military unit and civilian population, to survive in that surroundings. But that is probably a difference in opinion we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm just searching for motive. Do you agree that it looks different now, and perhaps the intention for -- to take Srebrenica was not the motive, rather, this information from the colonel on the ground. However, you have already responded to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. He answered the question. Please move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said -- actually, what do you think was the food situation in May 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: If you mean that the situation for the battalion in May -- well, it was low, but we still had stocks. Combat rations, if you mean the population, I know that the warehouse of the UNHCR in that period was empty, so the food that was present was only the food the people had themselves in their own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I had enough time, I would show you a document that we admitted on Friday. In May, the 28th Division appropriated almost 30 tonnes of flour, an tonne and a half of cooking oil, a lot of sugar, and many other products that we had allowed through in order for the population to obtain them when you say that there were food shortages. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I just stated what I recollect about the food situation in May. If there is a proof of any convoy coming in with food, I just don't recollect that. It's 17 years ago. I don't know every detail any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you fully aware -- or, rather, to what extent were you aware of the size and structure of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: What we knew at that time was that the 28th Division, being the former Operational Group, was organised in brigades, had a divisional structure, estimated strength 4-, 4.500 infantrymen, some mortars, and a couple of weapons -- weapon systems, including the T-55 main battle tank in the weapon collection point compound in Srebrenica where our B Company was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that they had at least two more tanks hidden in the hills and at least one self-propelled gun?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I did not know, and I doubt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I hope that we're going to show a document tomorrow showing how this equipment was being taken out. Did they take a tank from the storage facility in Srebrenica? Did they take it to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then if they were getting some tank and some self-propelled vehicle out, then that was a different piece of equipment altogether, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: If they were getting it out, it was equipment we were not aware of it. And again, based on the position of my observation post, the very moment these kind of vehicles would be deployed, I would have reports on that because it would have been without our -- within our observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Within the battalion, did you have an exchange of information, not only commanders and officers, but did your soldiers know about the environment that they lived and worked in? Did they know everything that the officers knew?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: If you mean information about the ABiH, they knew what we knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm concerned because some people who testified here said that they didn't know anything. They have either forgotten, or they didn't want to speak the truth. So you did not conceal the presence of a division there from them, a division consisting of four or five brigades; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a totally improper statement. Proceed with your questions, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I think that I do have the right to test what their -- what the previous witness has said. Their commander is saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are absolutely entitled to put questions what this witness knows, but not argue with this witness as to other witnesses's evidence. It is not now for you to make submissions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the agreement on the basis of which the Srebrenica protected area was established?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Generally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they give you a copy of that agreement with the map that showed the boundaries of that protected area as well as Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I can't remember seeing a copy of the full agreement, the text, I mean, but I got a map with the boundaries, the UN boundaries, of the Srebrenica enclave. On that map were also marked the Bosnian Serb boundaries and ABiH boundaries. There were, in fact, three boundaries, but we kept, as far as DutchBat is concerned, for us, of course, the UN boundaries were the correct ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This map, can one see on this map that the protected areas of Srebrenica and Zepa have a certain territory between them, a certain belt, if you will, that remained under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I know of that, but just to be clear, I never saw a map of Zepa and the exact boundaries. My knowledge is comprised to the boundaries of Srebrenica, and I'm aware of the fact that there was a corridor or space between the enclave of Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The corridor that linked them together or set them apart?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I probably used the wrong word. A corridor that set them apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that this corridor included the road between Podravanje and Skelani, or, rather, to Serb territories on the west, Milici, and on the east, Skelani, and the mine used that road?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I know much of the areas pretty good, but I can't exactly put Podravanje and Skelani in a place, but if you mean the road that was directly south or even at the edge of OP Echo, then to my map that part, let's say about 100 metres west/east, just in front of OP Echo was within the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why would we have signed such an agreement? Did somebody perhaps deceive you about this? Because when we signed the agreement we made sure that the road remained the territory we controlled, because they didn't need it and we did. Do you allow the possibility that somebody misrepresented the boundaries of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, it's speculation. I don't know whether there is a misrepresentation in the boundaries. I can only say how the boundaries were when we took over, and to me, that were the boundaries and that meant that, what, about 100 metres of that road were within Muslim territory. And if you state that it is a bad solution or idiotic, well, okay, but these are the facts. There was 100 metres of that road within the enclave, so not at this position of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm talking about, Mr. Franken. We never signed that map. In our map that was signed, the road was under our control, but we'll show that tomorrow. Tell us, did the Muslim side work to join and eventually manage to join the two enclaves, making them territorially continuous?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. I know that there was some illegal traffic between those two locations, between the enclaves, but I never had reports or any indications that they tried to really join them geographically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever get hold of Muslim military documents from Spring 1995 containing plans to join the two enclaves and also to join these two enclaves to the Tuzla region?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the civilian issues for a moment. You confirmed somewhere that the Serb side had suggested commercial co-operation and trade to be restored, but the Muslim side rejected that; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that one of the possible motives of that rejection was that the prices would fall and profits to be made on the black markets would be smaller?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I don't agree, but it is a possibility that that was a motive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you were certainly aware of the existence of the black market, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that this black market was not controlled by a pauper? It was controlled by the political and military leadership who had ways and means of protecting their own interests.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it's relevant what I believe or believed. We did some investigations in that direction to see whether and what amount the 28th Division was involved in the black market, but we couldn't find proof of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about that in your statement of the 26th and 27th September, 1995, on page 00443276 and 77 could we see that in e-court. Let me repeat. 00443276 and 77. Do we agree that your recollection was much fresher in 1995 than today?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's always true. Recollection in 1995 was better than in 2012.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This could be it. It's 1D04773. The ERN number should end in 276. That's it. And then the next page. Let us take a look. Did you give this statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Just wait. I'm trying to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we zoom in a bit.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is my statement - it's correct - about this trade. At least I see a part of it. I suppose it goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true what it says in the second paragraph, that the first few months there were no major incidents, or very few, and then: [In English] [As read] "In this period there was a proposal by the Serbs to do business with the Muslims according to the prices on the black market in the enclave. When I say business, I mean business in everything, except ammunition. After several rounds of negotiations, the civilian authorities of the enclave gave their approval for the goods to be supplied by the Serbs to the enclave. We visited that -- we insisted that the goods be sold in the enclave for roughly the same market price that DutchBat played -- paid," and so on. [Interpretation] Could we see the next page where you discuss who was involved in this. The civilian authorities were supporting it, if I'm seeing well, and the command of the 28th Division brought it down?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is: And now we see that during the first few months it was quiet without major incidents. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, it's just given the facts, there is not an explanation for the fact that in January, February, it was quiet, meaning incidents, armed incidents, just stating the situation. And I don't have an explanation for that, because the situation was the same that in the end DutchBat II was there, so there was no change in then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would the situation have been different for the civilian population in the enclave if the commercial and trade connections had been re-established?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I do think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted, at least these two pages?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2008, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D04767 is the next document I would like to call up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have the impression that the Muslims in Srebrenica were thinking only about the defence of their enclave, or they had active plans targeting Serb territories?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, I should give two answers. If you mean with the Muslims and referring to the normal civil population, they were only concerned in survival. The 28th Division, they did some -- I know of some attacks they did in Serbian territory. Whether they had plans or they had a strategy or whatever, I do not know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Take a look at this order of 27 May 1995. The 28th Division is ordering the 285th Brigade in Zepa to prevent the departure of civilians. To the best of your knowledge and in your experience, were the civilians willing to leave and go to some areas where they would live better, areas under Muslim control?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That thought or that will was never reported to me, and we didn't inquire anything in that direction, so I do not know whether they wanted to go in that period. There were no indications that they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is it true that they were trying to board UNHCR trucks when they returned empty, and many of them had put their names on waiting lists, wishing to leave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I do not know anything about boarding UNHCR trucks, and I know nothing about waiting lists or any organisation about leaving the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at the first paragraph which indicates that such a tendency existed and it was forbidden. And then look at paragraph 3. It speaks of armed control over the Serb territorial corridor between Zepa and Srebrenica. I don't want to read it out, but read at least the first ten lines of this paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I read it, and it is a pity I was not in that line of communications. Then I would have known in that time that those plans were there. But actually, in that period we were not aware of those plans or these orders. Again, I was not in the line of communication of the Bosnian Muslim army alas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have the impression that the sides were concealing certain things from the international community and its representatives?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not the impression. I had the conviction that it was so, because many times we asked the staff of 28th Division whether they had information. Perhaps you know that the intelligence information we got from the UN was close to zero. And then again, when we asked the Bosnian Serb army through Major Nikolic information, especially when he reported that there had been a raid by the Muslims, we got nilch [sic] on the report as well. We didn't get information. So although we knew they had information, they wouldn't give it to us, which means they concealed things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There's a conviction where we live that Serbs are poor hens, because hens, when they lay an egg, they trumpet it all over the place, whereas Serbs don't. So they probably did not take responsibility for this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit D2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you did know, or at least you heard rumours, that humanitarian aid is ending up in the hands of the army, the Bosnian army, and that the army is involved in its distribution and control?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: In answer to the first question, I know - I didn't hear rumours - but UNHCR told me, reported to me, and they consented in that, that the 28th Division took a part of the food supplies that came in by UNHCR. Whether the army - re: it the 28th Division - was involved in the distribution and control further for the other stocks, the resting stocks, I do not know. As far as I know, the "opstina," the civil element controlling the enclave, was responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that we had no obligation whatsoever to feed the enemy army or to allow that food and resources for the enemy army pass through our territory?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: What I understood is that what the 28th Division reserved for itself was for the families of the soldiers and the members of that division, because there were no barracks. They were still in their houses those soldiers. So of course the Serbs didn't have, what do you say, obligation in that way, but it was never a question that the Serbs had to bring food to the enclave. The UNHCR wanted and did, and the only role the Serbs played was consented, and then, I mean, the food was, in fact, for human beings, not only for the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps we could call it up, although you confirmed it already. Maybe I don't need the transcript. You said approximately the same thing in the Tolimir case and then in Popovic; Tolimir in 2010, and Popovic in 2006. But you confirm the same essentially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If there is no need, then you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we look at 65 ter 15563.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is before you came, but in our experience, it was uninterrupted, so by the time you arrived, we already had certain experiences and certain misgivings. So take a look at this document. Next page, please. I don't know why there are no more pages. It deals with the inspection of persons and weapons. Never mind. We'll remove this because it's obviously not the whole document. Can we see 65 ter 19464. 5D54. It must be chapter 5. [In English] Chapter 5, D54. [Interpretation] You were quoted here as concluding that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was more aggressive in inspecting convoys than the VRS, than the Army of Republika Srpska. Is it indeed what you reported?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can we just have that pointed out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Prosecution wanted the exact reference, but it's only chapter 4. I don't see any chapter 5 in this document. But without seeing the document, can you answer that question, Mr. Franken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I can, Your Honour. It's a strange quote, because I can't have said anything about the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina inspecting convoys because that was not the case, at least not in the period I was in Yugoslavia, in Srebrenica, and not as far as convoys meant for DutchBat III were concerned. They did not control within my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry, of what? Of chapter 4 or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 1: [In English] "The Bosnian Muslims, for their part, also impose restrictions on UNPROFOR's freedom of movement with the objective of controlling UNPROFOR and to be able to carry out operations without UNPROFOR's knowledge."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. My -- what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this part of the report of the Secretary-General correct? Did this indeed happen?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Within the enclave we had problems with freedom of movement in the so-called Bandera Triangle, piece of the enclave in the south-west.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see page 5 now. [In English] Fifth page out of seven. [Interpretation] That's the one. Paragraph 2: [In English] [As read] "It surprised Franken that UNHCR was not aware of the ABiH measures of checking convoys because he assumed that this had been passed on informally to -- by the Dutch liaison officer to the local UNHCR representative. However, MSF also appeared to be unaware of this measure."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, it can't be a convoy of vehicles. I never stated that because it is nonsense, as I tried to make clear before. The ABiH, within the enclave, never controlled anything about convoys or transports coming in or going out. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like the previous paragraph preceding that on page 4, the last part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I refer to the text, "It surprised Franken" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the top of page 5, so please take a look at the bottom part of the previous page, page 4. I think there's a reference to you, sir, "Major Franken explained this ..." could you take a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, this last paragraph here.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I'm reading. Just hold, please. This refers to a period in which we, more or less, controlled UNHCR convoys, because the ABiH claimed then, as is said in this paragraph, they wanted to control them because they were afraid that illegal things came in through UNHCR. We made then a kind of control just for the show to say we are doing that so you don't need to. Later on, the ABiH again threatened to make check-points within the enclave, which I forbade. That came to an incident, and when they still wanted to do that, I said that I would prevent that with all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see the next page. These convoy leaders were angry and the convoy inspections were supposed to take place on no man's land, and -- yes. Could you continue reading, please. Do we agree then that it's quite a way from Zvornik to Srebrenica all through Serbian-held territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry, I missed -- I just have -- I was reading. I'll just read the transcript. The route from Zvornik to Srebrenica is through Serbian-held territory. Yeah, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And inspections were only at the entrance to Zvornik and also at the entrance to Srebrenica; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is probable. I don't know exactly where those convoys were inspected. Earlier I stated that the UN convoys who came through -- mostly through another route were at least three times inspected. I was not part of those UNHCR convoys so I don't know, I was not reported where they were inspected in what way. As far as the text on the screen and on the page starting with the 20th of June, I doubt -- or, rather, I -- so it's incorrect that we should have search an UNHCR convoy more thoroughly than the VRS had done. Again, it was to show control to keep the ABiH quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For the first time you see that the Serbs ensured that only 100 to 150 litres of fuel remained in the truck so that there was nothing to be left in the enclave to the Muslim army; is that correct? This is one of those restrictions; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Whether that is right, I don't know. I see it here that how many litres remained, and, yes, you confirmed that one of the restrictions would be, as I gave on the convoys, was checking how much diesel was in the fuel tanks when they get in and how much there was in there when they come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that from the 15th of June, there was an offensive by the Muslim forces, first of all around Sarajevo, and that on June 20th when this convoy came with 56 tonnes of sugar, beans, salt, fish, and so on and so forth, flour, and so on and so forth, did the 28th Division carry out active combat in Serbian territory around Srebrenica in order to draw out the Serb forces and to make it easier for the Muslim army in Sarajevo? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I think I answered that, because you're saying that there was a convoy coming in and activity of the 28th Division increased. Again, I have no reports about that, and I don't have information about that. And if the 28th Division carried out its combat in Serbian territory, I'm not aware. I was not part of the decision-making, so I do not know what their strategy or their tactics or their objective was in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the top of the next page, please. Do you see here that the Muslim side also put some conditions to the UNHCR, and demands, and that there was a misunderstanding between them? Your name is mentioned. Somebody accused you of giving in to the Muslim side, and you said that you were not dancing to their tune; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I see that, but I do not recollect that, and I cannot imagine that I was dancing to anybody's tunes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Secretary-General said that you denied that, but obviously somebody did, but do you recall that the Serbian side had objections? And you can see now that the UNHCR also had objections regarding the UNPROFOR being a little bit more yielding in relation to the Muslims in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I can read the text. I don't know what the source of that text is. I do not recall this as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this, article 9 of chapter 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit it as Exhibit D2010.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us if you did a lot of shooting in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: If we did a lot of shooting in the enclave. Well, that is quite subjective. What is a lot of shooting? No, we did not a lot of shooting. On occasion when we were attacked we returned fire, if that is an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What were you spending your ammunition on and needed to replenish it, resupply it then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: First part of the answer is the situation when I came in was already that way, that we had a minimum amount of ammunition because when DutchBat I came in then already they were not able to bring all the ammunition that was needed. Ammunition tears -- that wears out, so to say, so in the situation when I came there I had about 16 per cent of the total amount of ammunition, which meant, for instance, that almost all my anti-tank capacity was not operational any more, because that ammunition couldn't be kept in a proper way, and it wears out if you have it in the field that long. It is sensible. And it is not only replenishing, it was, in fact, bringing the stock to the level that it should have been all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was worrying the Serbian side was where 84 per cent of the combat kit was spent. Where did -- if you had 16 per cent, where did the 84 per cent go, without having training practice, because that is something that would have disturbed both us and the Muslims; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I know that DutchBat II had some training practice, but again, 84 was never spent. The 84 per cent was never in the enclave. And that could have been 80 because there was some shooting training by DutchBat I and DutchBat II, but around 80 per cent never arrived in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it possible to rule out if not smuggling and sales then thefts? Do you know of instances of theft of Dutch equipment by the Muslims both in your battalion and the one before yours?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: To answer the last question, I do not know of any incidents like that in the period before DutchBat III. I recollect three times with one attempt to steal equipment from OPs. Those were temporary OPs. And then ammunition was not involved. It was always they tried to steal a can of diesel fuel or something like that. Two were successful, one not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since you are aware of the LiveNote, the transcript, in your previous answer you meant that DutchBat also had some training practice, not specifically DutchBat number II. The first line, "I know that ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's referring to the use of ammunition. DutchBat III did not train with ammunition in that period because we had that little ammunition, but DutchBat I and II, the two battalions were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the first line of your answer DutchBat II should read DutchBat II also.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "I know the Dutch ..." You mean the answer, "I know that DutchBat II had some training practice"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That should be DutchBat I and II had some training practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at 1D04741 [Realtime transcript read in error "1D4074"] now, please. Is it correct that the Muslim side counted on your military alliance and that it was making preparations to act together with you against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I do not know how and in what esteem they counted on our military alliance. I know that I had a conversation, and I look to the date, 31st of May. Yes, that must have been in May where I had a conversation with the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division where he asked me what DutchBat would do when the Serbs attacked the enclave. End of that -- that discussion was that I said we would defend our observation posts, and he said that the 28th Division would defend the area between the observation posts. So there is -- being a UN unit, I could not really co-ordinate any defence, of course, but there is in that way some co-ordination in the case that the Bosnian Serb Army would attack the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Just to interrupt. I just to make sure the record is clear. At line 15 it should be 1D4741.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not sure, but that is that document, but very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that Mr. Oric was outside of the enclave on the 31st of May and that he did not come back since March and that this Ramiz Becirevic was standing in for him, his Chief of Staff of the 28th Division; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at these paragraphs together then. In the first one that there should be a test. In the second that they should conceal weaponry from you, that you don't see what they have. These are just bullet points. In the third one, to be convincing and to fight, then an order to order the mortar trenches on all axes, and then to begin us, the Dutch Battalion to give you back the ammunition and infantry weapons that we handed over so that we would have a true picture if they were our allies but to do it without the knowledge of the observers. And then it says do not agree with the Dutch dissolving their depot from their headquarters to other locations because it will enable them or it might be a trick intended to leave us without ammunition, and knowing what is in store for them it would give them an excuse to say the Chetniks took it, and so on and so forth. All right. Well, when this falls into our hands on the 31st of May, can you imagine what we are thinking about your co-operation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I can imagine anything. There's a simple solution for that: Ask us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2011, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at 1D976, please, so that we can see how two days after that measures are enforced in relation to you. You can see on the 2nd of June to the command of the 285th Zepa, from the division command, it says: With reference to your document written confidential, and so on and so forth, we here give you all the following instructions: Cover all UN check-points with our forces and do not allow UN troops to cross over to the Serbian side. In case UN troops attempt to leave Zepa they are to be disarmed and captured and their weapons and hardware put to use in the defence of the territory. Assure the UNPROFOR commander in Zepa, Colonel Dudnjik, of our good intentions and co-operation and convince him to withdraw explosives from the check-points. Let him know that we are prepared to defend both ourselves and then in the event of an attack. Also use the civilian organs of authority to give him this assurance. Ban any kind of contact between UN soldiers and unauthorised personnel. So, is it clear to you now why the Serbian Army was concerned about the weaponry and equipment you were bringing into the enclave, because at any point they could fall into the hands of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this document refers to the situation in Zepa and the UN unit in Zepa. Yeah. Why the Serbian Army was concerned about what, I do not know. I do not think there was any reason in Srebrenica, because you could be sure that under no circumstances I would give our equipment and weaponry to any party in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps not voluntarily, but would you hand them over if 5.000 of Oric's soldiers surrounded you and made you do that? What would you do in such a situation? What could you do in that situation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I can't answer that question because that depends on the situation: How the grouping is, in what terrain, et cetera, et cetera. I can't give an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2012, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at 65 ter 30734. Either I didn't say the number properly or something else is in question. It's not a transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please be asked to repeat the last two numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 03734.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And this should be the last question for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I please draw your attention to the text. We will soon see a translation. This is an analysis of the Army of Republika Srpska on the 10th of July before the capture of the enclave about events that preceded it. Could you please look at all the things that were going on before you and also in the months before the month of July.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I could, and I have to read it. Just hold, please. I read it that far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we look at the next page, please. It states here the UNPROFOR is entirely informed about the Muslim terrorists and overall military activities and is not preventing them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we please know where Mr. Karadzic is reading from.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Franken can read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm trying to, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is this: Is there a possibility or another explanation for the first action which the Serbs halted even though they could have continued with it? And in this case, in this one when the Serbs halted and entered Srebrenica only when the 28th Division left it, is there another explanation, too, about what you said how the Serbs made a breakthrough? My Serb -- my thesis is that the Serbs did not have a plan to enter Srebrenica and that they entered Srebrenica in July because the 28th Division had pulled out completely and the town had been emptied; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the units that were in the town, did they clash?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: You're referring to what units? ABiH units clash with each other you mean? I see you nod. No, they did not clash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we'll --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to clarify this question, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the 28th Division defend the town street by street? Were they fighting to keep the town, or did the 28th Division withdraw before the Serbs reached the town?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: To give a complete answer, the 28th Division fought its way back to town from the confrontation line, UN confrontation line. Then, as I recollect well, in the evening of the 10th, they were still in defensive positions around Srebrenica, and as far as I know, they left in the night of the 11th, in the early morning of the 11th. Then they withdrew from Srebrenica. But before that the Bosnian Serb army attacked, actually, Srebrenica. Even my forces opened fire on them when they came down the hill. Then they withdrew.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We will clarify this further tomorrow. I would like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2013, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. Probably you are already aware of this, but you're not supposed to discuss with anybody else about your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 17th day of January, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.
